transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (CTO, Pioneer), Rina Shah (Platform Eng), Oliver Park (APIs Lead)

Summary:
- High-level integration discovery for Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for Pioneer Payments
- Primary concerns: latency SLOs, data residency, SDK support (LangChain / LlamaIndex), gateway/proxy architecture, rate limits and quotas, and observability hooks
- Agreed next step: Redwood to send pricing/TCO, sample integration snippets, and schedule a technical deep dive for infra team

Topics: SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy, rate limits/quotas, observability hooks, benchmarking

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood. We got Maya from our SE team as well. Could we do quick intros?
[00:08] Carlos: Sure, Carlos Mendes, CTO at Pioneer. We run payments infra for small merchants, lots of PCI scope.
[00:12] Rina: Rina Shah, platform, I look after our API gateway and deployments.
[00:16] Oliver: Oliver Park, lead on APIs and SDKs.
[00:20] Maya: Hi all, Maya Patel, I focus on integrations and performance at Redwood.

[00:35] Jordan: Cool. High level, Pioneer is evaluating whether Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private makes sense. Today maybe start with integration questions, especially about SDK support, LangChain and LlamaIndex, and the gateway/proxy pattern you mentioned in the signup.
[00:47] Carlos: Yeah, we have two POCs right now. One is a checkout assistant that needs sub-150ms tail lat for small prompts, and another is a reconciliation job that can batch. Primary worry is PCI and data residency, and also not wanting to manage the whole model infra ourselves.
[01:05] Rina: Also-- we have an existing API gateway (Kong) and we usually front any third-party with a proxy for auth and rate limiting. Question is how Redwood expects customers to integrate when we use LangChain or LlamaIndex in server-side flows.

[01:25] Maya: Good, thanks. For LangChain/LlamaIndex we provide SDKs in Python, Node, and a direct HTTP REST API. Most customers either use our SDK directly or plug Redwood as the llm provider in LangChain with a small adapter. The pattern is: your server calls Redwood SDK, or you can use a local gateway that proxies requests to Redwood for central auth and observability.
[01:45] Oliver: When you say adapter, is it officially supported? We've seen community adapters but they break on streaming and function calling.
[01:52] Maya: We have maintained LangChain adapters in our github repo and a LlamaIndex example. The adapters support streaming and function calling, but small caveat: some community libs change APIs, so we version our examples and pin to LangChain x.y where we validated behavior. I'll share snippets.
[02:10] Jordan: Note: link to repo will be in the follow-up.

[02:20] Carlos: About gateway/proxy-- we need to keep all requests logged inside our VPC and with our auth flow. Can we run a lightweight proxy in our VPC that the SDK talks to and that proxy forwards to Redwood Hosted? Any gotchas?
[02:34] Maya: Absolutely. Many customers run a proxy in front of Redwood. For Hosted it's a common pattern: the proxy handles SSO, adding headers, and auditing. The proxy can also implement rate limiting and key rotation. We recommend adding a mutual TLS or per-request signing if you want to reduce risk. For Dedicated/Private, you can also terminate inside your VPC so traffic never leaves.
[02:57] Rina: How about latency; if we add a proxy, will that push us over the 150ms tail?
[03:03] Maya: Depends on network hops and the model choice. For short prompts we're seeing single-digit ms server overhead on Highland GPUs but end-to-end is network + model. Recommended approach: colocate the proxy in same region as Redwood endpoint and use persistent connections. We'll help with benchmarking.

[03:25] Oliver: Rate limits and quotas -- how granular are they? We have a multi-tenant stack inside Pioneer, and we want per-merchant quotas and throttles at the per-key and per-route level.
[03:36] Jordan: On Hosted we expose API keys and usage quotas per key and per org. For more granular per-merchant controls we recommend placing your own proxy which enforces per-merchant quotas and mapping to a single Redwood key, or for Dedicated you can configure per-route policies in our console for your teams.
[03:52] Maya: Also mention token-level billing, you can map quotas to token budgets. If you need per-merchant accounting we can surface token-level logs to your SIEM or S3.

[04:08] Carlos: Observability hooks -- what do we get? We have strict audit and need traceability to user and request ids.
[04:15] Maya: We emit request-level metadata: request_id, model, prompt_size, token_count, latency, nodes traversed. For Hosted we provide logs via secure S3 exports, and CloudWatch/BigQuery integrations. We also have tracing hooks compatible with OpenTelemetry. For Dedicated you can pull raw telemetry with higher retention.
[04:37] Rina: Is there PII in logs; how is that handled?
[04:40] Maya: By default we redact PII fields if you enable our data-protection toggles, and Hosted customers can opt out of retaining prompts. For compliance we support customer-managed keys for encryption-at-rest in Dedicated or Private.

[04:56] Oliver: On SDKs, how do you support streaming and function calls in Python? Any snippet?
[05:02] Maya: Yes example snippet: use our python SDK client.ChatStream and register a callback for tokens. For LangChain, you set RedwoodLLM as provider and enable stream=True; for function calling we map the JSON schema through our tool-calling hooks. I'll attach code.
[05:18] Jordan: Quick note: our SDK also supports a lightweight gateway mode so you can run local validation before forwarding. It's useful for rate limiting on a per-merchant basis.

[05:35] Carlos: About Dedicated vs Hosted: we care about predictable throughput and SLA. Our peak is about 800 RPS for small token exchanges during Black Friday like spikes, but normal is 50-100 RPS. Can Dedicated handle that level?
[05:50] Maya: Yes, Dedicated instances are sized by GPU pools and we can set autoscaling policies with burst capacity. We'll need to size based on your exact token distribution; that's why we asked for sample traces for benchmark. With proper batching we can keep unit cost low while hitting SLOs.

[06:08] Rina: If we go Dedicated, what network topology do you recommend? VPC peering or private link? We prefer traffic not routed over the public internet.
[06:16] Maya: For Dedicated we support PrivateLink and VPC peering depending on cloud. For on-prem or air-gapped we have a Private deployment package. We can provide an architecture diagram in follow-up.

[06:30] Oliver: Any limitations with LangChain when we use tools or chain-of-thought prompts? Sometimes context windows blow up.
[06:37] Maya: If you need larger context we suggest two things: memory management via KV-cache and prefix caching, which our runtime supports, and also reranking flows so you only hit the model for top-k candidates. LlamaIndex is useful for vector retrieval pre-filtering. Both patterns are in our example repo.

[06:55] Carlos: Security review questions: SOC2, ISO, support for SSO/SAML, RBAC?
[07:01] Jordan: We are SOC2 Type II and have ISO docs. SSO via SAML/OIDC supported for Console, RBAC via granular roles, and audit logs. For Dedicated/Private we offer customer-managed KMS. We'll include our security pack link.

[07:20] Rina: How do you do canary rollouts and model version pinning? We need safety when model updates happen.
[07:25] Maya: Console supports model pinning per-route, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to a pinned variant if regressions occur. We also support evaluation hooks where you can tie prompt-sets to quality monitors and alert on regressions.

[07:45] Oliver: One more on quotas: If we hit a limit, what's graceful degradation? Does Redwood return standard 429 or provide suggestions backoff headers?
[07:53] Jordan: We return 429 with X-RateLimit headers and a Retry-After. For Dedicated you can configure soft and hard limits and auto-burst policies that fall back to lower-capacity variants.

[08:06] Carlos: Cost question: how does quantization affect latency and quality? We want to save cost but not regress on chargebacks classification.
[08:13] Maya: Quantized variants can reduce memory and per-token cost; quality depends on model and quant level. We recommend running a small eval suite against your prompts; Redwood Optimize will analyze regressions and recommend quantization profiles.

[08:30] Jordan: Sounds like action items are clear. We'll share pricing and snippets. Any other blockers?
[08:36] Carlos: Only one--legal. We'll need DPA and PCI scopes.

[08:39] Jordan: DPA and PCI addenda are standard; we'll share them.

[08:45] Rina: For the benchmark, if we provide sample traffic and keys, will Redwood run an in-region benchmark or do we need to run load from our side?
[08:54] Maya: We can run both. We typically provide a harness that you can run inside your VPC to mimic production traffic, and we can also run a supervised benchmark from our side with synthetic traces. We'll coordinate on the best approach.

[09:10] Oliver: Any gotchas with LlamaIndex's indexing step? We prefer serverless indexing but worry about cold starts.
[09:16] Maya: Indexing often benefits from pre-warming and persistent store for embeddings; Redwood recommends caching embeddings or using our embedding endpoints with caching policies. We'll include examples for incremental indexing.

[09:35] Jordan: Alright, let's recap next steps. Jordan to send TCO/pricing and security pack, Maya to share LangChain/LlamaIndex snippets and observability doc, and Pioneer to provide perf targets and sample data for benchmark. We'll set up a deep technical call week of 2026-03-09.
[09:58] Carlos: Sounds good, thanks.
[10:02] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite and links.

End of transcript.
